prompt: Why did inserting at position 0 cost the `ArrayList` hundreds of milliseconds and the `LinkedList` a few?
hint: Think of what has to move.

choices.text: The `ArrayList` reallocates and copies its whole backing array on every single insertion
choices.why: It grows its array only when it is full, by half again; the cost here is the shifting.

choices.text: Each insertion shifts every element already in the array one slot right
choices.why: Right: the hundred-thousandth insertion moves 99,999 references; the linked list changes two links.

choices.text: `LinkedList` stores `int` values directly, without boxing them
choices.why: Both hold `Integer` objects; neither stores primitives.

choices.text: The JIT compiles the `LinkedList` loop and not the other
choices.why: Both loops run hot; the difference is in the work each operation does.

prompt: `LinkedList.get(i)` took seconds over a hundred thousand calls. What does one call do?
hint: There is no array to index.

choices.text: It copies the list into an array and indexes that
choices.why: Nothing is copied; it follows links.

choices.text: It searches the list for the element equal to `i`
choices.why: That would be `indexOf`; `get(i)` wants the element at position `i`.

choices.text: It walks node by node from the nearer end
choices.why: Right: up to fifty thousand steps per call for a hundred thousand elements.

prompt: A program builds a list of loans once and then reads it by position thousands of times. Which class?
hint: Which operation dominates?

choices.text: `ArrayList`
choices.why: Right: reading by position is one step, and building it at the end is cheap.

choices.text: `LinkedList`, because it was built by adding
choices.why: Adding at the end is cheap for both; the reads are what cost, and they cost the linked list a walk each.

choices.text: Either: both implement `List`, so they cost the same
choices.why: They keep the same promise at very different costs; section 02 measured it.

choices.text: `TreeSet`, so that the reads are sorted
choices.why: A set drops duplicates and has no positions; two loans of one book would become one.

prompt: In `List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();` the declared type is the interface, and only the word after `___` names the class.
hint: The keyword that creates the object.

prompt: `Orders.java` put seven titles, two of them repeated, into a `HashSet`. How many came out, and in what order?
hint: A set keeps each element once.

choices.text: Seven, in the order they went in
choices.why: The repeated `Dune` and `Emma` were dropped, and insertion order is `LinkedHashSet`'s.

choices.text: Five, in alphabetical order
choices.why: Five is right; alphabetical order is `TreeSet`'s.

choices.text: Five, in an order the class does not promise
choices.why: Right: `Beloved, Dune, Ulysses, Middlemarch, Emma`, which is whatever the buckets produced.

prompt: Match each set to the order it keeps.
hint: The table in section 03.

pairs.right: No order you can rely on

prompt: `BrokenKey` printed `size 2`, `contains false` and `equal? true`. What single change made it print `size 1` and `contains true`?
hint: `equals` was already right.

choices.text: Replacing `HashSet` with `ArrayList`
choices.why: A list keeps duplicates by design, so `size` would stay 2.

choices.text: A `hashCode` built from `isbn`, the field `equals` compares
choices.why: Right: equal books then land in the same bucket, where `equals` can see them.

choices.text: Making `isbn` a `final` field
choices.why: It already was `final`; the missing piece was the hash code.

choices.text: Adding `@Override` above `equals`, so that the compiler checks its signature
choices.why: It was already there, and it only makes the compiler check the signature.

prompt: Two `Book` objects are `equals` but have different hash codes. Which statement about a `HashSet` holding one of them is true?
hint: The hash code chooses where to look.

choices.text: `contains` with the other one is `true`, because `contains` calls `equals`
choices.why: `equals` only runs inside the bucket the hash code picked, and that is the wrong bucket.

choices.text: Adding it throws an exception
choices.why: Nothing checks the contract; the set just quietly holds both.

choices.text: Adding the other one gives two entries
choices.why: Right: different hash codes send them to different buckets, so the set never compares them.

prompt: A test prints a `HashSet<String>` and compares the result with a fixed string. It passes today. What is wrong with it?
hint: What did the class promise about order?

choices.text: It relies on an order `HashSet` never promised
choices.why: Right: the same elements print the same way until the table resizes or the elements change.

choices.text: Nothing: a `String`'s hash code is fixed, so the order is too
choices.why: The hash codes are fixed; the order also depends on the table's size, which grows with the set.

choices.text: Printing a set calls `hashCode`, which is slow
choices.why: `toString` walks the set; the speed is not the problem.

prompt: In `Counts.java`, what did `count.merge(title, 1, Integer::sum)` do the first time it met `Dune`?
hint: The key was absent.

choices.text: It threw, because there was no value to add 1 to
choices.why: `merge` handles the absent key itself; that is why it replaces the hand-written test.

choices.text: It stored `1` under `Dune`
choices.why: Right: absent key, so the given value goes in; later calls add 1 to it.

choices.text: It stored `0`, and the second loan made it 1
choices.why: The map ended with `Dune=3` for three loans, so the first one counted.

choices.text: It called `Integer.sum(null, 1)`
choices.why: The function only runs when there is an old value to combine with.

prompt: `int n = count.get("Beloved");` runs, and `Beloved` is not in the map. What happens?
hint: `get` printed `null` for it.

choices.text: `n` is 0, because a missing `int` takes its default value
choices.why: Defaults apply to fields; here `null` is unboxed into an `int`, and that fails.

choices.text: A `NullPointerException`, unboxing the `null` that `get` returned
choices.why: Right: `getOrDefault("Beloved", 0)` is the way to say what absent means.

choices.text: A compile error, because `get` returns `Integer`
choices.why: Auto-unboxing makes it compile; the failure waits for run time.

prompt: To group titles by first letter, `byLetter.___(title.charAt(0), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(title)` returns the list for the key, creating it first if there is none.
hint: Compute it if it is absent.

prompt: A `HashMap<Book, Loan>` uses a mutable `Book` whose `hashCode` reads its title. A book is put in, then its title is corrected. What does `get` with that same object answer?
hint: Where was the entry filed?

choices.text: The loan, because it is the very same object
choices.why: The map looks in the bucket the new hash code picks, and the entry is in the old one.

choices.text: Very likely `null`, though the entry is still in the map
choices.why: Right: it sits in the bucket of the old hash code, where no lookup goes.

choices.text: A `ConcurrentModificationException`
choices.why: That is about changing a collection while iterating it, lesson 34; nothing iterates here.

choices.text: The map rehashes the key automatically when its field changes
choices.why: The map has no way to know a field changed.

prompt: A program must answer, for each loan request, whether that ISBN is already reserved. Which interface fits the question?
hint: "Is this one in there?"

choices.text: `List`
choices.why: A list answers by position; `contains` on it reads every element.

choices.text: `Set`
choices.why: Right: membership is the question a set is built around.

choices.text: `Queue`
choices.why: A queue answers which one leaves next.

choices.text: `Deque`
choices.why: A deque is a queue open at both ends; it still does not answer membership quickly.

prompt: Why does the section prefer `List<Book> loans = new ArrayList<>();` to `ArrayList<Book> loans = new ArrayList<>();`?
hint: What can the rest of the program call?

choices.text: The first form runs faster, because interface calls are cheaper
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the object is the same `ArrayList` either way.

choices.text: The second form does not compile
choices.why: Both compile; the diamond works with either declared type.

choices.text: It limits every later call to the methods of `List`
choices.why: Right: with only `List` methods in use, changing the class later is one word after `new`.

prompt: Which of these are good reasons to choose a `TreeMap` over a `HashMap`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Pay for an order only when something reads it.

choices.text: A report prints the entries sorted by key
choices.why: Yes: the sorted order is read, so it is worth its comparisons.

choices.text: The map will hold a great many entries
choices.why: Size alone favours the hash map, whose lookups do not compare along a tree.

choices.text: The program asks for the first key after a given one
choices.why: Yes: `ceilingKey` and its relatives exist only on sorted maps.

choices.text: The keys are strings
choices.why: Strings work as keys of either map.

prompt: A loan screen needs the borrowed titles in the order they were borrowed, each title once. Which class?
hint: Once each, and an order that is not sorted.

choices.text: `ArrayList`
choices.why: It keeps the order and also the duplicates.

choices.text: `TreeSet`
choices.why: Once each, but in sorted order, not the order of borrowing.

choices.text: `HashSet`
choices.why: Once each, in no order you can rely on.

choices.text: `LinkedHashSet`
choices.why: Right: uniqueness from the set, insertion order from the list through its entries.

prompt: `Counts.java` saw six loans of three titles. How many entries did the `HashMap` named `count` hold at the end?
hint: One entry per key.

prompt: Put the steps of `shelf.contains(book)` on a `HashSet` in the order they happen.
hint: Two steps decide it, after one call.
items: The hash code picks a bucket
`equals` compares `book` with each element in that bucket

prompt: A program keeps reserved ISBNs in an `ArrayList<String>` and calls `contains` on every request. It is slow with fifty thousand reservations. What is the smallest correct change?
hint: The collection is doing a set's job.

choices.text: Switch it to a `LinkedList`, which is faster to search
choices.why: Searching is a walk in both lists; the linked one is not faster at it.

choices.text: Keep them in a `HashSet<String>` instead
choices.why: Right: `contains` then jumps to a bucket instead of reading every element.

choices.text: Sort the list once and keep calling `contains`
choices.why: `contains` on a list does not know it is sorted; it still reads element by element.
